craft_claim: Bitter irony lands by echoing a prior claim or norm the reader can recover and marking it with a dissociated attitude; cynical deflation therefore needs a stated ideal to work against, not inversion for its own sake.

supporting_evidence.note: Sperber's echoic-mention account treats verbal irony as echoing an actual or attributed thought while signalling a dissociated attitude toward it; irony is interpretive rather than literal reversal.
The echoic-reminder model predicts sarcasm is most accessible when a prior expectation or norm is available to be echoed; the ironic line requires a shared benchmark the audience can recall.

Gibbs found sarcastic utterances are understood against the situation and prior expectation rather than decoded literally and then reversed, so ironic force depends on a recoverable context, not on inversion mechanics.

supporting_evidence.location: Whole collection (maxims on virtue, friendship, and self-esteem)
supporting_evidence.note: Each maxim re-describes an admired motive as a form of self-love, deflating a professed ideal the reader already holds; the echoic prior is the social claim, not an uttered sentence.

counterevidence.note: Sections G and H record that sustained barbed, ridiculing delivery reads as hostility and tracks poorer relational outcomes, so an echoic deflation can be mechanically correct and still fail by taxing the reader-writer relation; flat delivery carries farther than barbed because it lowers the hostile signal.

scope: Ironic and deflating voice across fiction, essay, and copy; strongest where a prior ideal is culturally shared.
exceptions: Rival accounts of irony (pretense, dissociation) differ in mechanism but converge on the craft requirement of a recoverable prior.
Where no shared norm exists to echo, the same device reads as arbitrary contrarianism rather than recognition.
